Common Name:  Sailfin molly
Scientific Name:  Poecilia latipinna

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Poeciliidae
Other Common Names:  Sailfin

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Lesueur, 1821)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sailfin mollies have been used as aquarium fish (Hoedeman 1974).
Recreational:  This molly is kept by hobbyist in home aquaria (Hoedeman 1974).
Ecological role:  The sailfin molly is one of the most important fish in impounded wetland habitats along the Indian River Lagoon.  This species was third in overall numerical abundance, overall weight, and percent occurrence (Lewis et al. 1985; Gilmore 1987).  In the trophic study conducted by Harrington and Harrington (1961), the majority of fish eaten by piscine predators in that wetland were sailfin mollies.
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The sailfin molly is found in coastal fresh, brackish, and salt waters from southeastern North Carolina to northwestern coast of Yucatan peninsula, Mexico (Rosen and Bailey 1963).
Within Study Area:  The sailfin molly is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon system in estuarine and freshwater wetlands (Gilmore 1977).
Life Mode:  This livebearing euryhaline species can be found in a wide variety of habitats anywhere in the water column in groups generally feeding on vascular plants, algae, or plant detritus (Harrington and Harrington 1961, 1982; Snelson 1980; Loftus and Kushlan 1987).
Mobility and Migration: In the Indian River Lagoon, the sailfin molly utilizes the annual fall sea level rise (Provost 1974) to invade seasonally flooded wetland habitats  (�high marsh�) and produce a peak annual abundance in this area (Gilmore 1987).  As the water levels subside in November and December, the mollies move back into the deeper tidal creeks and marsh ponds.

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
The sailfin molly occurs in a variety of shallow vegetated habitats including freshwater streams and canals, mainland and barrier island wetlands (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1977, 1988).  This species is generally associated with submerged or emergent vegetation and/or periphyton and is not commonly found in open deeper waters with little vegetational cover (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1977; Loftus and Kushlan 1987).  Mollies occur in the entire water column traveling in small to moderate sized groups (Loftus and Kushlan 1987).
Substrate:  Sailfin mollies can be found over sand, mud, marl or sediments with large amounts of detritus in association with vegetation or periphyton (Gilmore 1977; Snelson 1980; Loftus and Kushlan 1987)

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Sailfin mollies are euryhaline surviving in salinities from 0 to 70 ppt (Gilmore et al. 1982; Loftus and Kushlan 1987).
Temperature: Mollies in the Indian River Lagoon can survive temperatures from 4 to at least 35 C and dissolved oxygen levels below 1 ppm (Snelson 1980; Gilmore et al. 1982, unpub. data).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The sailfin molly is a gonochoristic, iteroparous,  polygamous livebearer; eggs are fertilized internally (Snelson et al. 1986; Constantz 1989)
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs throughout its range in the Indian River Lagoon with successful reproduction occurring from February to as late as November in the northern portions of the Lagoon (Snelson 1980).  Spawning season may be longer in the southern Lagoon.  Reproduction ceases when water temperature exceeds 32-35 C (Snelson 1980).  Spawning peaks occur in the spring and fall with a midsummer depression in activity (Snelson 1980).  Females can produce multiple broods in a single season with interbrood intervals ranging from 21 to 68 days with an average of 34 days (Snelson et al. 1986).  Mature males range in size from 16 to 103 mm with small males depending on forced insemination while larger dominant males use aggressive behaviors to deny small males access and courtship behaviors to elicit female cooperation in mating (Snelson 1985; Travis and Woodward 1989).  Females can store sperm and fertilize successive broods from one mating (Snelson 1980), however single broods may be sired by multiple males (Travis et al. 1990).
Fecundity: The number of developing embryos averages from 6.4 to 40.5 young per brood.  Number of embryos increases with size of the female (Trexler 1985; Reznick and Miles 1989).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Mature eggs are clear amber in color and reach a diameter of approximately 2.2 mm.  Upon reaching maturity, eggs are fertilized within the ovarian follicles (Snelson et al. 1986).  Embryogenesis continues until young are fully formed.  Length of gestation period is temperature dependent and ranges from 23 to 27 days at 26-28 C (Snelson et al. 1986).
Juvenile:  Neonates are born fully formed at lengths averaging 5.7 to 9.8 mm (Snelson 1982) and may take from 50 to over 200 days to reach maturity (Travis 1989).
Adult:  Males grow very little after reaching maturity and size at maturity varies widely from 16 to over 50 mm (Trexler 1986).  Age at maturity varies in the same way with small males maturing first.  Females mature generally  between 22 and 37 mm (Snelson 1980, Reznick and Miles 1989).  Age at maturity can range from 50 to over 200 days (Travis 1989).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Sailfin mollies are generally herbivorous consuming vascular plants, algae, and plant detritus.  Small juveniles may consume copepods.  When mosquito larvae are present in great number, they may represent over 50% of the food volume (Harrington and Harrington 1961, 1982).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The sailfin molly is one of the most important fish in impounded wetland habitats along the Indian River Lagoon.  This species was third in overall numerical abundance, overall weight, and percent occurrence (Lewis et al. 1985; Gilmore 1987).  In the trophic study conducted by Harrington and Harrington (1961), the majority of fish eaten by piscine predators in that wetland were sailfin mollies.

Mobility and Migration: In the Indian River Lagoon, the sailfin molly utilizes the annual fall sea level rise (Provost 1974) to invade seasonally flooded wetland habitats  (�high marsh�) and produce a peak annual abundance in this area (Gilmore 1987).  As the water levels subside in November and December, the mollies move back into the deeper tidal creeks and marsh ponds.

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
The sailfin molly occurs in a variety of shallow vegetated habitats including freshwater streams and canals, mainland and barrier island wetlands (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1977, 1988).  This species is generally associated with submerged or emergent vegetation and/or periphyton and is not commonly found in open deeper waters with little vegetational cover (McLane 1955; Gilmore 1977; Loftus and Kushlan 1987).  Mollies occur in the entire water column traveling in small to moderate sized groups (Loftus and Kushlan 1987).
Substrate:  Sailfin mollies can be found over sand, mud, marl or sediments with large amounts of detritus in association with vegetation or periphyton (Gilmore 1977; Snelson 1980; Loftus and Kushlan 1987)

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: Sailfin mollies are euryhaline surviving in salinities from 0 to 70 ppt (Gilmore et al. 1982; Loftus and Kushlan 1987).
Temperature: Mollies in the Indian River Lagoon can survive temperatures from 4 to at least 35 C and dissolved oxygen levels below 1 ppm (Snelson 1980; Gilmore et al. 1982, unpub. data).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  The sailfin molly is a gonochoristic, iteroparous,  polygamous livebearer; eggs are fertilized internally (Snelson et al. 1986; Constantz 1989)
Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs throughout its range in the Indian River Lagoon with successful reproduction occurring from February to as late as November in the northern portions of the Lagoon (Snelson 1980).  Spawning season may be longer in the southern Lagoon.  Reproduction ceases when water temperature exceeds 32-35 C (Snelson 1980).  Spawning peaks occur in the spring and fall with a midsummer depression in activity (Snelson 1980).  Females can produce multiple broods in a single season with interbrood intervals ranging from 21 to 68 days with an average of 34 days (Snelson et al. 1986).  Mature males range in size from 16 to 103 mm with small males depending on forced insemination while larger dominant males use aggressive behaviors to deny small males access and courtship behaviors to elicit female cooperation in mating (Snelson 1985; Travis and Woodward 1989).  Females can store sperm and fertilize successive broods from one mating (Snelson 1980), however single broods may be sired by multiple males (Travis et al. 1990).
Fecundity: The number of developing embryos averages from 6.4 to 40.5 young per brood.  Number of embryos increases with size of the female (Trexler 1985; Reznick and Miles 1989).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Mature eggs are clear amber in color and reach a diameter of approximately 2.2 mm.  Upon reaching maturity, eggs are fertilized within the ovarian follicles (Snelson et al. 1986).  Embryogenesis continues until young are fully formed.  Length of gestation period is temperature dependent and ranges from 23 to 27 days at 26-28 C (Snelson et al. 1986).
Juvenile:  Neonates are born fully formed at lengths averaging 5.7 to 9.8 mm (Snelson 1982) and may take from 50 to over 200 days to reach maturity (Travis 1989).
Adult:  Males grow very little after reaching maturity and size at maturity varies widely from 16 to over 50 mm (Trexler 1986).  Age at maturity varies in the same way with small males maturing first.  Females mature generally  between 22 and 37 mm (Snelson 1980, Reznick and Miles 1989).  Age at maturity can range from 50 to over 200 days (Travis 1989).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Sailfin mollies are generally herbivorous consuming vascular plants, algae, and plant detritus.  Small juveniles may consume copepods.  When mosquito larvae are present in great number, they may represent over 50% of the food volume (Harrington and Harrington 1961, 1982).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: The sailfin molly is one of the most important fish in impounded wetland habitats along the Indian River Lagoon.  This species was third in overall numerical abundance, overall weight, and percent occurrence (Lewis et al. 1985; Gilmore 1987).  In the trophic study conducted by Harrington and Harrington (1961), the majority of fish eaten by piscine predators in that wetland were sailfin mollies.
